description: The bar chart illustrates the “Popularity” of knowledge across three domains — Movies, Songs, and Basketball — as perceived by three large language models (LLMs): Llama3 (blue, solid fill), ChatGPT (red, solid fill), and an unnamed third model represented by yellow bars with diagonal stripes. The vertical axis, labeled “Popularity,” ranges from 0 to 220 in increments of 20. For each domain, the chart displays five grouped bars representing different combinations of accuracy and ground truth (GT) annotations: “Acc=0 & GT Ans” (blue with diagonal stripes), “Acc=0 & Gene Ans” (red with diagonal stripes), “Acc=1 & GT Ans” (yellow with diagonal stripes), and two additional categories represented by solid blue and red bars (Llama3 and ChatGPT, respectively), though their exact mapping to accuracy conditions is not explicitly labeled in the legend. In the “Movies” category, popularity values are relatively low, with Llama3 and ChatGPT both around 30–40, and the striped bars ranging from 20 to 50. In “Songs,” popularity increases, with Llama3 and ChatGPT reaching approximately 70–90, and the striped bars ranging from 40 to 70. In “Basketball,” popularity peaks significantly: Llama3 reaches ~180, ChatGPT ~210, and the yellow striped bar (Acc=1 & GT Ans) reaches ~170, while the other striped bars are around 100–140. The chart suggests that popularity scores vary substantially by domain and model, with Basketball showing the highest perceived popularity across all models and conditions, and the striped bars generally showing lower popularity than the solid-colored model bars, especially in Basketball. The legend also includes “Acc=0 & GT Ans” and “Acc=0 & Gene Ans” with striped patterns, indicating these represent incorrect answers (accuracy=0) associated with ground truth or generated answers, while “Acc=1 & GT Ans” represents correct answers. The chart visually emphasizes that higher popularity correlates with correct answers and specific domains like Basketball, potentially reflecting how knowledge popularity influences LLMs’ perception of their own knowledge boundaries.
